Milan Aftabuddin Ahmed ------ For the Petitioner 
Md. Anser Ali with Basiruddin Miah ------ For the Opposite parties

Md. Reazul Karim ------Petitioner
Vs.
Mst Shirin Begum ------Respondents
full_judgment:
This Rule was obtained by the petitioner who was O.P. No. I in a preemption case to revise the concurrent judgments and other passed by the original and the appellate court below refusing the present petitioner's claim for rateable preemption under section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 2. The present O.P. being the petitioner brought the case for preemption under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Her case was that Kalipada Roy was the original owner of the holding from whom she purchased .33 lands by kabala Ext. A(1) dated 28.7.75 and thereby she became a co-sharer in the holding Kalipada Ray sold some other lands of the holding to Gita Rani Roy who being thus a co-sharer of the holding sold 164 land to the present petitioner by kabala Ext. A dated 21.11.75. The present O.P. as a co-sharer filed the preemption case on 11.4.78 while the kabala Ext. A which was sought to be preempted was registered on 17.12.77. 

 3. The present petitioner who was O.P. No. 1 pleaded the case to be barred by limitation and alternatively stated that he had purchased 19 and from the original owner Kalipada by Ext. A(1) which was a document executed on 21.11.75 and registered on 17.12.77 and thus he became already a co-sharer in the holding as the registration number of his kahala was 24655 while the registration number of the kabala sought to be preempted being subsequent was 24656. Accordingly he claimed rateable preemption under section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by making such prayer in the written objection within two months of knowledge of the preemption case as no notice of the said case was served on him. 

 10. It is an established principle of law that a kabala after it is duly registered takes effect not on the date of registration but on the date of execution. In this case undisputedly the present petitioner's kabala Ext. A(1) which is a registered document was executed on 21.11.75. This means that the present poi-OM got his right in the lands of Ext. A(1) on 21.11.75. In other words, be became a co-sharer in the holding on 21.11.75. On the other hand it is also a settle law that a cause and right of preemption accrues only after a kabala which is sought to be preempted is finally registered. In this case the kabala Ext. A which is sought to be preempted was admittedly registered and entered in the volume on 17.12.77. So the cause and right for preemption of this kabala accrued for the first time on 17.12.77 when this kabala was entered in the volume and registration completed under section 60 of the Registration Act. As I have already found, the present petitioner became a co-sharer on 21.11.75 while the cause and right for preemption accrued on 17.12.77 that is two years after. This being so the present petitioner undoubtedly became a co-sharer in the holding two years before. So it is immaterial that the two kabalas was executed and registered on the same date and the question as to the time of execution and registration of the kabalas are equally immaterial. Thus it is found that the present petitioner was entitled in law to claim rateable pre-emption under the provision of section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 

 11. Mr. Anser Ali further submitted that since the petitioner did not submit any application under section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act to claim rateable pre-emption and also when contrarily the preset petitioner opposed the case of pre-emption he could not be allowed to claim rateable preemption. In support of his contention Mr. Anser Ali referred to a decision of the appellate Division in the case of Nur Banu Vs. Nur Mohammad reported in 35 DLR (HD) (1983) page 182. In that case it was held that when a defendant by her written statement discarded a document being fraudulent she could not be allowed to take any plea in her favour by reference to such document. This decision cannot be said to apply to the facts of the present case which is quite different. In this case the present petitioner being O.P. No. 1 resisted the claim for preemption by the plea of limitation and at the same time made an alternative claim for rateable preemption in case the preemption was allowed by holding the case not to be barred by limitation 

 12. Regarding the plea of Mr. Anser Ali that a separate application to claim rateable preemption under section 96(4) was necessary this is not acceptable. According to section 96(4) a co-sharer tenant including the transferee could apply to seek rateable preemption. In this case though no separate formal application was submitted nevertheless the present petitioner being O.P. No. 1 had clearly stated that in his written objection that he seeks rateable preemption. In the case of Afazuddin Mridha and others Vs. Mobarakullah and others reported in 5 DLR page 254 it has been held by this court that a prayer of the transferee co-sharer opposite party in his written objection that she may be allowed to preempt proportionate to her share in the tenancy is a sufficient compliance with the provision of sub-section 4(a) of section 26F and a formal application is not necessary. Section 96(4) is quite similar to section 26F(4) of the B T. Act. So following the same proposition I hold that in this case the present petitioner having sought rateable preemption by making sub prayer in the written objection this was a sufficient compliance of section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.
